newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sags, bourses mixed despite Wall St.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sags, bourses mixed despite Wall St.

text.p: The dollar sagged in early European trade on Wednesday, while Wall Street's record-breaking performance failed to spark an answering bounce in Europe's share markets.

Both French and German shares fell in early business following Tuesday's intraday records, but London made some gains following Wall Street's late surge to a record 7,067 points on the Dow Jones index.

On the bond markets, German government bonds started a a touch lower after bond futures stormed to a series of new highs on Tuesday. In London, government gilts spiked lower at the start then recovered after stronger than expected retail sales figures for January.
The dollar's soggy start was blamed by traders on the German Bundesbank and Japan's trade surplus showing an underlying uptrend.

The dollar was also undermined by mark trading against other major currencies, with the lira taking another beating following mounting concerns that Italy will miss the first wave of countries joining a single European currency in 1999.
The lira slumped to a three-month low of 999.60 per mark before recovering to 996.15 by 1015 GMT.

In its February report, the Bundesbank said the mark's strong rally since the start of 1995 had more than corrected, while the central bank's president Hans Tietmeyer was quoted as saying he hoped the dollar's rise against the mark was over.

"The rise of the dollar against the mark in recent weeks was a normalisation of exchange rates which has been due for a long time. I hope that this correction has now come to an end," Tietmeyer told Germany's Bild newspaper.
The dollar was quoted at 1.6892 marks at 1015 GMT after an early morning dip towards support at 1.68. Dollar/yen was trading at 123.70 compared with 123.94 at the European close on Tuesday.
Although the Japanese non-seasonally-adusted trade surplus dived by 91.7 percent in January from a year earlier, analysts said the surplus was up 25.6 percent on a seasonally-adjusted basis.

"Despite the fact that the headline rate was down compared to a year ago, the underlying picture shows exports are doing well, and in particular exports with the U.S. are on an improving trend," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB.

Elsewhere, the peseta slipped against the mark again, prompting the Bank of Spain to buy pesetas for marks, dealers said. The Swiss franc clawed back a little against the dollar but sank to its worst level against the mark in more than three years.
Sterling, which had a bruising day on Tuesday, firmed against the mark and dollar in morning trade.
In contrast to French and German share markets, London opened higher, getting a boost from Wall Street and the overall weakening of the pound which should ease pressure on exporters.

The FTSE 100 index nudged to its best levels of the day as the retail sales figures helped the bond market hold firm. But traders said caution remained ahead of U.S. consumer prices due at 1330 GMT. The FTSE was up 10.9 points, or 0.25 percent, at 4,343.2.

Dealers said any sign of stronger-than-expected U.S. growth could send bonds lower and spell an end to recent stock market gains, although the benign interest rate backdrop was likely to underpin markets on both sides of the Atlantic.
SmithKline Beecham led drug stocks higher amid positive comment on its results on Tuesday, its shares leaping 23 pence to 917.5 by mid-morning.

"We are going up today with this rally on Wall Street but the interesting question is by how much," said one dealer. "With the pound coming off as talk of rising interest rates recedes, there are pretty powerful reasons for the market to go up."
The German DAX index opened bourse trade sharply lower, tracking Tuesday's post-bourse slide after the dollar slipped from its 34-month highs.
